Disasters leave no time to negotiate how help arrives.

As devastating floods in Nepal show, damaged infrastructure and difficult access can make reaching people in need an immense challenge.

If these things can be defined before a disaster happens, governments and humanitarian organizations can focus on the response. - Jagan Chapagain, IFRC Secretary General

That is why the IFRC is calling for Earth’s Missing Treaty: a global disaster treaty to strengthen preparedness, protect people most at risk and establish clear rules for humanitarian assistance to cross borders.

We must act before the next disaster strikes.
items.author: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

items.text:
There is a missing treaty! 🚀🌍

Humanity has made treaties to protect and regulate many things, from migrating birds to coffee crossing borders to astronauts returning safely to Earth.

In 1968, governments created the Rescue Agreement, requiring countries to help astronauts in distress and return them safely.

Nearly 100 states have joined that agreement.

But there is still no equivalent treaty for people facing disasters. No global agreement setting out clear obligations before, during and after emergencies.

That is ifrc campaign Earth’s Missing Treaty! 

Learn more at EarthsMissingTreaty.org
#EarthsMissingTreaty

We don't get many astronauts in this briefing room. They are here to brief you on the new IFRC disaster research campaign launch: "Astronauts at the heart of push for the world's first international disaster treaty." And she is wearing her uniform, so that's even more interesting.

L'an dernier, 360 catastrophes naturelles ont été dénombrées dans le monde, qui ont impacté 110 millions de personnes et ont coûté 170 milliards de dollars en pertes économiques.

Depuis le tsunami en Asie de 2004, les ONG réclament un traité international pour permettre une meilleure coopération entre États lors de catastrophes. Pour convaincre les pays de l'adopter avant la fin de l'an prochain, la Fédération internationale des sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge a lancé une campagne jeudi 3 septembre.

Publié le : 04/09/2026 – 09:42

2 min Temps de lecture

Publicité

Lire la suite

Avec notre correspondante à New York, Carrie Nooten

Dylan Winder, le représentant de la Fédération internationale des sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge (IFRC) à l'ONU, le sait : certains accords d'assistance mutuelle régionaux ou bilatéraux existent déjà. Mais ils ne suffisent pas. L'anticipation est d'autant plus primordiale qu'elle réduit par 15 le coût d'une catastrophe naturelle pour un État.

Pourtant, les produits de secours d'urgence sont encore soumis en moyenne à 17 % de taxes, sans compter qu'ils mettent en moyenne onze jours à passer la douane. Le traité réclamé par les ONG depuis le tsunami de 2004 vise précisément à lever une partie de ces obstacles. « En raison des contraintes administratives, certaines licences sont nécessaires pour faire passer des marchandises en douane, explique Dylan Winder . Il faut également des visas pour permettre au personnel de se rendre sur place, si besoin. Anticiper ces démarches permet de gagner du temps ; surtout que nous savons que durant les 72 heures suivant une catastrophe – en particulier un séisme –, ce gain de temps sauve des vies. »

items.text:
Les astronautes en détresse bénéficient depuis des décennies d'un cadre international visant à leur porter secours. Mais lorsqu'une catastrophe frappe sur Terre, aucun traité mondial ne définit encore les règles de coopération entre Etats. La Croix-Rouge veut combler cette lacune.

Depuis 1968, un traité international oblige les Etats à porter secours aux astronautes en détresse. Près de 60 ans plus tard, aucun équivalent mondial n'existe encore pour organiser l'aide aux populations frappées par une catastrophe ici bas.

C'est sur ce paradoxe que la Fédération internationale des Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge ( IFRC ) a bâti sa nouvelle campagne, lancée jeudi et intitulée Earth's Missing Treaty (« Le traité manquant de la Terre »). Son objectif : pousser les Etats à conclure le premier traité international global consacré à la protection des personnes avant, pendant et après les catastrophes.

L'Accord sur le sauvetage des astronautes, entré en vigueur en 1968, oblige notamment les Etats parties à secourir et assister les astronautes victimes d'un accident ou en situation de détresse.

« S'il existe un traité qui protège les personnes qui redescendent de l'espace, nous avons aussi besoin d'un traité sur Terre qui protège ceux qui s'y trouvent », a résumé jeudi Dylan Winder, observateur permanent de l'IFRC auprès des Nations Unies, lors d'une conférence de presse à New York.

Derrière la formule se cache un problème beaucoup plus prosaïque. Lorsqu'une catastrophe survient, l'aide internationale peut se retrouver prise dans un dédale de douanes, de taxes et de procédures administratives précisément au moment où chaque heure compte.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies issued the following news release:

* * *

Astronauts at heart of new IFRC campaign for world's first international disaster treaty

International treaties protect astronauts in distress. But if a flood strikes your city, there is still no comprehensive global treaty to help countries cut through red tape and coordinate international assistance.

New York/Geneva - The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) is today launching a new global campaign, Earth's Missing Treaty, to highlight a stark reality: while international law protects astronauts in distress, there is no comprehensive international treaty setting out how countries should cooperate to protect people before, during and after disasters.

The campaign highlights IFRC's call for countries to support the adoption of the Treaty on the Protection of Persons in the Event of Disasters, which UN Member States have agreed to negotiate and which would be the first comprehensive global treaty dedicated to protecting people before, during and after disasters.

A global treaty would provide a common framework for international cooperation before disasters strike and when international assistance is needed. In practice, this could mean faster deployment of humanitarian teams, simpler customs and border procedures for life-saving supplies, more predictable cooperation between governments and humanitarian organisations, lower costs and fewer administrative barriers, and better protection for people affected by disasters.

Alongside the campaign, IFRC is publishing new global analysis showing why a disaster treaty is needed and the difference it could make. The research brings together data on disaster risk, protection and barriers to international assistance, alongside four country case studies from Belize, Fiji, Lebanon and Madagascar.

Read the case studies for Belize, Fiji, Lebanon and Madagascar.

Noon briefing of 3 September 2026 UN80 INITIATIVE Today, the U.N. General Assembly adopted a resolution endorsing the merger of the U.N.

System Staff College (UNSSC) and the U.N. Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR).

The Secretary-General is expected to speak to the UN General Assembly today at 3:00 p.m. to discuss progress of UN80.

U.N. SYSTEM STAFF COLLEGE / U.N. INSTITUTE FOR TRAINING AND RESEARCH MERGER

The Secretary-General welcomes the U.N. General Assembly's decision to merge the United Nations System Staff College with the United Nations Institute for Training and Research, replacing them with a single new entity: the U.N. Institute for Capability and Learning Innovation (UNICLI). This decision is an important step towards the Secretary-General's UN80 Initiative, and part of the broader consolidation of the U.N. system's training and research capacities. The adoption of this decision during the 80th session of the General Assembly carries particular significance.

This decision creates a stronger, a more integrated platform of learning and capability development, and institutional transformation.

It recognizes that capability and development, continuous learning, and innovation are not ancillary functions, but strategic drivers of UN's effectiveness and reform, and impact for Member States.

The Secretary-General invites Member States, the U.N. entities, partners, and all stakeholders to join the U.N. in shaping the new entity's future and strengthening its contribution to a more sustainable, inclusive, and resilient world.

NEPAL

Tom Fletcher, Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator has allocated an additional $500,000 from the U.N.'s Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) to the humanitarian efforts in Nepal. This brings the total CERF funding following the disaster to $2.5 million.

O objetivo é concluir as negociações e adotar o tratado até o final de 2027, unificando padrões e procedimentos para facilitar a cooperação entre governos e organizações humanitárias, reduzir custos e simplificar processos administrativos.

La Fédération internationale des Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge (FICR) a lancé une campagne mondiale pour l'adoption d'un traité visant à coordonner l'aide internationale en cas de catastrophe.

La FICR a annoncé cette campagne intitulée « Traité manquant pour la Terre » lors d'une conférence de presse au siège des Nations unies à New York jeudi.

L'aide internationale en cas de catastrophe est actuellement fournie au niveau régional ou sur la base de traités bilatéraux et sectoriels. Cependant, les efforts consentis se heurtent souvent à des obstacles administratifs, tels que le dédouanement, qui retardent l'acheminement des secours.

La nécessité d'un traité mondial global est débattue depuis le tsunami de 2004 dans l'océan Indien.

Lors de la conférence de presse, les représentants de la FICR ont évoqué la récente catastrophe au Népal. Ils ont souligné qu'un traité international permettrait d'établir des règles claires pour l'aide internationale en cas de catastrophe et d'aider les gouvernements et les organisations humanitaires à simplifier les procédures administratives et à agir plus rapidement, garantissant ainsi que l'aide parvienne plus vite aux populations.

Ils ont ajouté que le projet de traité stipule que les pays ont le devoir de prévenir, d'atténuer et de se préparer aux catastrophes, par des mesures appropriées telles que la mise en place de systèmes d'alerte à l'avance.

Les responsables ont indiqué que les négociations sur le projet avaient débuté en avril et que les pays membres de l'ONU s'étaient engagés à conclure les pourparlers d'ici la fin de l'année prochaine.

COLOMBO (News 1st); The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) has voiced strong support for a proposed global

treaty aimed at improving international cooperation and protecting people affected by disasters, describing it as a historic opportunity to strengthen disaster preparedness and response worldwide.

Speaking at the United Nations, IFRC Permanent Observer Dylan Winder said the initiative highlights a longstanding gap in international law, noting that while international treaties exist to protect astronauts in distress, there is still no comprehensive global treaty dedicated to helping countries coordinate assistance when disasters strike on Earth.

"The idea behind the campaign is simple. International treaties protect astronauts in distress. But if a flood strikes in your city, there's still no comprehensive global treaty to help countries cut through red tape and coordinate international assistance on Earth," Winder said.

He noted that UN member states are expected to come together next year to negotiate the Treaty on the Protection of Persons in the Event of Disasters, a move he described as a landmark moment for global humanitarian cooperation.

"This represents a historic opportunity that we at the IFRC are pleased to be supporting with our decades of experience in disaster preparedness and response," he said.

Winder stressed that when major disasters overwhelm a country's ability to respond, bureaucratic and administrative barriers can delay the arrival of humanitarian personnel, specialized equipment, and life-saving supplies.

According to him, a global treaty would provide a common framework for international cooperation before disasters occur and when international assistance becomes necessary.

After two decades of work, a treaty could see the light of day next year, sketching out the rules for how countries help each other when disaster strikes. But they still have to overcome old divides over its implications for sovereignty and human rights.

Last week, mud and floodwater tore down the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli river corridor in Nepal, flattening villages, roads and bridges in their path. More than 4,200 people are still unaccounted for while more than 1,200 have been confirmed dead. In the months before, the earth shook with violent force under Venezuela and Colombia, trapping scores of people under the rubble.

Each time, rescue efforts quickly got underway – the first hours and days are critical for survivors. Proposals for assistance from states, NGOs and diaspora communities poured in just as fast. These latest events are a stark reminder that when disaster strikes, international coordination is critical. Yet, there are no global rules on how countries should work together before, during and after a natural or man-made disaster.

States are hoping to change that, with a new UN treaty expected to be adopted as soon as next year. “There are many instruments at the regional or sector level that provide for disaster response and cooperation, but there is no overarching comprehensive international legal framework, and this really will fill that gap,” said Isabelle Granger, global lead for disaster law and auxiliary role at the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), speaking from preparatory meetings this week in New York.

The network of humanitarian national branches, often at the frontline of disasters, has been pushing for the initiative for years and is now providing technical assistance.

La Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (IFRC) y un grupo de astronautas exigieron este jueves en la ONU impulsar el primer pacto global que proteja a las personas ante las catástrofes naturales.

"Los tratados internacionales protegen a los astronautas en apuros. Pero si una inundación sacude tu ciudad, todavía no existe un tratado global integral que ayude a los países a recortar la burocracia y coordinar la asistencia internacional en la Tierra", indicó Dylan Winder, observador permanente de la IFRC ante la ONU, en una rueda de prensa en la sede de Naciones Unidas en Nueva York.

Más de una decena de astronautas se han sumado a la iniciativa, entre ellas Sian Proctor, quien también es geocientífica, y que destacó cómo los países se unen para proteger misiones en el espacio pero no en la Tierra.

Winder señaló que solo el año pasado se produjeron más de 350 desastres relacionados con fenómenos naturales que afectaron a más de 110 millones de personas y generaron pérdidas por valor de 169,700 millones de dólares.

"Tan solo 24 horas de aviso previo ante un peligro inminente pueden reducir los daños resultantes hasta en un 30%, y cada dólar invertido en la reducción del riesgo de desastres y la resiliencia puede ahorrar alrededor de 15 dólares en pérdidas futuras", añadió.

Según comentó, la mortalidad es seis veces menor en los países que cuentan con sistemas integrados de alerta temprana.

"En catástrofes como la de Nepal, un tratado mundial establecería normas claras para la ayuda internacional y ayudaría a los gobiernos y a los agentes humanitarios a sortear los trámites burocráticos con mayor rapidez", enfatizó.

La IFRC lamentó que aunque existen acuerdos regionales, bilaterales y sectoriales falta un tratado internacional que unifique normas y procedimientos.

items.text: La Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (FICR) y un grupo de astronautas solicitaron a las Naciones Unidas promover el primer pacto global destinado a proteger a las personas de desastres naturales. Se destaca la falta de un tratado global integral para ayudar a los países a coordinar la asistencia internacional en caso de desastres naturales, a pesar de que existen tratados internacionales que protegen a los astronautas en peligro. Más de una docena de astronautas se han unido a la iniciativa, enfatizando la necesidad de un tratado global para proteger misiones en la Tierra. Se mencionó que la anticipación de peligros naturales puede reducir daños hasta en un 30%, y que la inversión en reducción del riesgo de desastres puede ahorrar hasta $15 por cada dólar invertido en futuras pérdidas. La FICR lamenta la falta de un tratado internacional que unifique estándares y procedimientos para agilizar la asistencia humanitaria en casos de desastres. Las negociaciones entre países para adoptar el tratado se iniciaron en abril con el objetivo de concluir el trabajo y adoptar el tratado para finales de 2027.

items.text:
Disasters do not stop at borders, and neither should our ability to help people. Every hour lost to legal and administrative barriers can cost lives. Earth has treaties for the skies, the seas and even outer space. 

Today, I am very proud to announce that the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies - IFRC is launching a new global campaign, Earth’s Missing Treaty, to highlight a stark reality: while international law protects astronauts in distress, there is no comprehensive international treaty setting out how countries should cooperate to protect people before, during and after disasters. The campaign highlights IFRC’s call for countries to support the adoption of the Treaty on the Protection of Persons in the Event of Disasters, which UN Member States have agreed to negotiate and which would be the first comprehensive global treaty dedicated to protecting people before, during and after disasters.

We are calling on governments to seize this historic opportunity and create the world’s first international disaster treaty, putting people first when they need help most. https://lnkd.in/eYNhd2BG
